mediaItem.itemTitle: Wrongful Conviction False Confessions - SPECIAL UPDATE
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This special breaking news episode of "Wrongful Conviction: False Confessions" focuses on the issue of police deception during interrogations and its role in eliciting false confessions. Host Laura Nyreiter interviews Marty Tankliff, a New York exoneree who falsely confessed to murdering his parents at age 17 after police lied about evidence.  Illinois State Senator Robert Peters discusses his sponsorship of Senate Bill 2122, aiming to ban deceptive interrogation tactics in Illinois. Dave Thompson, a police trainer, explains why lying is unnecessary and harmful, advocating for ethical and evidence-based interrogation methods. The episode highlights the need for legislative change to protect innocent individuals and improve the integrity of the justice system, urging listeners to support bills in Illinois, New York, and Oregon.

keyQuotesRaw: Marty Tankliff: "Well, if my father said I did it, maybe I did, because my father's never lied to me, and police aren't supposed to lie to you." (Illustrates the impact of authority figures and deception on false confession.)
Marty Tankliff: "They made me [confess]." (Describing the coercive nature of the interrogation.)

Senator Robert Peters: "What happened to Marty's damn shame, and I'm sorry that you had to go through that, Marty. And what is so painful is that it's not surprising. We see this all the time." (Highlights the systemic nature of the problem.)

Dave Thompson: "No, there's other methods that they can be trained in, which we can discuss. The law needs to change. And we also know it increases the fear of innocent people, like Marty just described..." (Advocates for change and ethical interrogation methods.)

Dave Thompson: "It looks like asking open-ended questions, a conversation where the investigator doesn't have a goal of a confession, but has a goal of obtaining actionable and reliable information..." (Describes ethical interrogation approach.)
systemicIssuesRaw: Police deception during interrogations as a common practice leading to false confessions.
Training of police officers in deceptive tactics.
Lack of legal prohibition against police lying in interrogations in most US states.
Power imbalance and vulnerability of young people and other individuals during interrogation.
Confirmation bias of investigators leading to tunnel vision and focus on obtaining a confession rather than truth.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Support for legislation banning police deception during interrogations (specifically mentioned bills in Illinois, New York, and Oregon).
Call to action for listeners to contact legislators and support these bills.
Promotion of ethical and evidence-based interrogation methods that do not rely on deception.
Retraining of police officers in non-deceptive interrogation techniques.
personalNarrativeRaw: Marty Tankliff's personal experience of wrongful conviction and false confession highlights the devastating impact on individuals and families.
His story serves as a powerful example of the harm caused by deceptive interrogation tactics.
Marty's resilience and advocacy for change after exoneration are emphasized as inspirational.
Marty's current work as an attorney and adjunct professor, teaching students to reinvestigate wrongful conviction cases, demonstrates his commitment to systemic change.
